import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.fx

@torch.jit.script
class Helper:
    @torch.jit.export
    def hello(self):
        print("hello")

class M(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.helper = Helper()

frozen = torch.jit.freeze(scripted, preserved_attrs=['helper'])

📚 Documentation
https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.AvgPool2d.html writes
divisor_override – if specified, it will be used as divisor, otherwise kernel_size will be used

which implies that  torch.nn.AvgPool2d(2, divisor_override=2) should be equivalent to torch.nn.AvgPool2d(2) (which it is not).
torch.nn.AvgPool2d(2)(torch.ones(1, 4, 4))
tensor([[[1., 1.],
         [1., 1.]]])
torch.nn.AvgPool2d(2, divisor_override=2)(torch.ones(1, 4, 4))
tensor([[[2., 2.],
         [2., 2.]]])

I suggest using something like the more correct explanation given here:
https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.nn.functional.avg_pool2d.html.

🚀 Feature
Support comparisons between c10::optional<T> and U if T is comparable to U.
Motivation
A very common use-case for this is:
c10::optional<std::string> opt = ...;
if (opt == "blah") ...

Note that this is supported by std::optional. See https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/optional/operator_cmp
under

Compare an optional object with a value

Pitch
Add support and testing for these additional overloads. These are expected to just replace the operators that look like:
template <typename T>
bool operator==(std::optional<T> const& opt, T const& val);

with
template <typename T, typename U>
bool operator==(std::optional<T> const& opt, U const& val);

Alternatives
This makes the library more expressive. The alternative with existing functionality is if (opt && *opt == "blah") ....
Additional context
This is not expected to be a significant amount of work (< one day).

Our linter scripts are scattered across numerous ad-hoc scripts. A large part of our linter logic is also encoded inside of .github/workflows/lint.yml. These features make it difficult to re-use logic, thereby making it both bug-prone and cumbersome to express more complex linter workflows. Further, ad-hoc scripts do not enable a good user experience, making it harder for users to detect and debug flakiness.
Here are some examples of the mentioned issues:

File filtering logic

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/actions_local_runner.py#L165-L172
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/linter/clang_tidy/run.py#L376-L460
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/linter/clang_format_all.py#L33-L44
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/.github/workflows/lint.yml
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/linter/clang_format_all.py#L33-L44


Running shell commands

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/linter/clang_tidy/run.py#L173-L195
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/linter/clang_format_all.py#L57-L59
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/tools/actions_local_runner.py#L105-L130


Error reporting

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/.github/workflows/lint.yml#L117-L123
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/.github/workflows/lint.yml#L391-L399


Multiple ways to run lints

make <lint name>
python3 tools/linter/<linter name>
Commit hooks
python3 tools/actions_local_runner.py <lint name>


Dependency requirements are scattered

Proposal
I'm proposing that we consolidate our linter scripts into a single framework (written in Python) that supports common operations like file filtering, running lints on changes, running shell commands, and reliable error reporting. The lints will be exposed through a dispatcher script that will invoke the appropriate linter and report back results.
Once we have this, we should migrate all of the logic from within .github/workflows/lint.yml to this new framework, thereby making python scripts the source of ground truth. The new .github/workflows/lint.yml would simply invoke the dispatcher script and report back errors (if any)
Goals

Support only one way to run linters
Make it easier to run lints locally
Provide an ergonomic way to run lints
Enable code re-use and linter extensibility

This is how I envision the usage to be:
alias lint="python3 tools/linter/lint.py"

# Run all lints on the codebase
lint

# Run all lints only on changes
lint --changed-only

# Run a single lint on the codebase
lint mypy

# Run a single lint configured with options
lint clang-tidy --paths torch/csrc --diff-file pr.diff --verbose
Once we have this dispatcher script, we can use it to create a setup.py lint target, which is advantageous as PyTorch devs use setup.py to build their code.
Implementation
I have a WIP PR (#62393) that implements the aforementioned infrastructure.
It provides a Lint base class. Each linter is implemented in a separate module. The module must expose a class that extends the Lint base class. Each linter declares the options it accepts (this includes things like file filters, verbose output, extra arguments). The dispatcher script with take the declaration, instantiate the linter, and run it.
Related issue: #62370
Future vision:

Possibly release our framework as a separate package
How can we support existing linter workflows?

The pull request #61678 added an argument allow_empty_param_list to _FunctionalSGD. If allow_empty_param_list=True, then the optimizer does not raise a ValueError upon an empty parameter list.
Overlapping DistributedDataParallel.backward() with ZeroRedundancyOptimizer.step() relies on using a functional optimizer as the local optimizer for ZeRO. Moreover, the current design has ZeRO share the same bucketing strategy as DDP. As a result, for certain configurations, there may be fewer buckets than ranks, in which case some ZeroRedundancyOptimizer instances have an empty shard of the parameters (i.e. they do not need to update any shard of the parameters). (An example is ResNet-50 with bucket_cap_mb=25 yields 5 buckets, so training on 8 GPUs will have 3 ranks with empty parameter lists.)
One approach is to detect the empty parameter list in ZeroRedundancyOptimizer logic and modify the behavior. However, since the new OptimizerHookState class introduced in the aforementioned PR seems to expect an allow_empty_param_list argument for all functional optimizers, a simpler solution would be to follow through and add that argument to the remaining optimizers. In that case, ZeroRedundancyOptimizer does not need to modify its logic to check for an empty parameter list explicitly.
The changes would take place in functional_adadelta.py, functional_adagrad.py, functional_adam.py, functional_adamax.py, functional_adamw.py, functional_rmsprop.py, and functional_rprop.py.

🐛 Double sign error at density transformations
These docs correctly state the following:
Let f be the composition of transforms applied::
        X ~ BaseDistribution
        Y = f(X) ~ TransformedDistribution(BaseDistribution, f)
        log p(Y) = log p(X) + log |det (dX/dY)|

but in this line the following is calculated (in pseudo code):
log p(Y) = log p(X) - log |det (dX/dY)|
This would give wrong values, but it seems that the method log_abs_det_jacobian (for example here ) returns the wrong sign in every implementation I have seen.
In the linked example the determinant of the jacobian of log(y) is 1/y. Consequently, the log of it is - log(y) = - x and not x.
For all current implementations, this double sign error cancels out and has no consequence.
But every user, who is unfamiliar with this bug, will implement the log_abs_det_jacobian with the correct sign at first, which will give wrong results.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Implement the correct log_abs_det_jacobian function in a Transform class.
Create a transformed density with this Transform class.
Compare the log density values of the implementation with the real log density values.

Expected behavior
It is expected that a TransformedDistribution subclass with the correctly implemented Transform class returns the correct log density values.

Overhead

Profile both functions with record_function and compare times --> first function is much faster now

PyTorch’s CI has many moving parts, any of which can fail and cause churn on PRs or master, confusing devs and reducing trust in our tests. The CI has grown organically over time, so there are likely places that can be improved with a concerted effort.
Survey
Most of the things in this issue are just ideas without any real data to back them up or track over time. We should have some way of measuring the complexity of our CI and track that over time. Things could include:

Number of CI jobs
Number of conceptual steps per job (i.e. not just the steps as the CI platform defines, but any time we switch runtimes (i.e. a bash script → a bash script → a Python script)). It’d be cool if we could assemble a big graph of these and visualize everything in one place
Configuration length - This is a pretty indirect measure, but the more logic we push from platform specific definitions to Python scripts, the more flexible we become and the easier it is to understand what is happening when our CI runs

Possible Improvements

Remove Jenkins - We currently maintain 3 CI platforms - GitHub Actions, CircleCI, and Jenkins. We only host a single ROCm build on Jenkins and it’s not clear that it’s necessary to maintain a third CI system when we can use custom runners with GitHub Actions

Migrate pytorch-linux-bionic-rocm4.2-py3.6-* jobs to GitHub Actions with a custom runner
Remove ci.pytorch.org and jenkins.ci.pytorch.org DNS entries
Shut down (but don’t terminate) the Jenkins and Worker EC2 instances

If everything is fine after some period of time, we can permanently decommission these


Remove Jenkins logic from the HUD


Consolidate on Python in CI - Many of our build scripts are a combination of CircleCI/GHA dispatching logic, a few bash scripts, then finally a Python harness. Migrating these bash scripts to Python will improve cross-platform running (no need for batch scripts) and be more approachable to PyTorch devs.
Use templates / community GitHub Actions for common patterns

We have some common steps that are duplicated in a bunch of places in our GitHub Actions workflows: Chown workspace, archive / store artifacts, clean up docker images, Parse ref. We could make more liberal use of Jinja templates so these could be defined in one place, and for actions that fit the pattern we could write custom actions like with https://github.com/seemethere/upload-artifact-s3


Migrate nightly and viable/strict pushes from internal FB infra to GitHub Actions cron jobs

🚀 Feature
torch.nonzero should accept an optional size argument to produce statically shaped output to (1) avoid host-device synchronization and (2) avoid truncating CUDA/LazyTensor IR graph during tracing.
Motivation
Because the number of nonzero elements is data-dependent, we currently fetch the number of nonzero elements from device, and allocates the corresponding output tensor using the shape information at host runtime. To make the shape information available at host, a host-device synchronization is injected after the fetch of an integer, which stalls the pipeline between Python frontend and device runtime, and also breaks the CUDA/LazyTensor IR graph as we need actual execution to correctly get the concrete shape information and continue the tracing.
Pitch
Similar to the nonzero API in JAX, we add a size argument to torch.nonzero:

If specified, the first size nonzero elements will be returned; if there are fewer nonzero elements than size indicates, the index arrays will be zero-padded.

In addition to zero-padding, we could also return a counts device tensor to specify the number of nonzero elements at runtime. Similar to what NVIDIA did to enable CUDA graph in MaskRCNN-ResNet50 MLPerf training benchmark v1.0.
Alternatives
Add a runtime_shape tensor field to the tensor class, which will require all ATen operators to be aware of the possible divergence of runtime shape (as tensor of integers on device) and statically inferred shape bound (as c10::IntArray).
Additional context
The following operators either directly call at::nonzero or have similar machinery:
index.Tensor
masked_select
_unique2
nms

PyTorch-XLA encodes the runtime shape information in the opaque tensor handle and does not truncate IR graph. However, it is not sound when users inspect output.shape in Python which is merely a statically inferred shape bound.
torch.jit.trace does shape erasure to support dynamic shape when shape dynamism does not alter the IR graph.

Future of Windows Smoke Tests
To save on CI cost while maintaining a level of signal quality, we currently run a small subset of test cases (instead of the full test suite) on Windows CUDA configs on PRs. An example can be found here for the pytorch-win-vs2019-cuda10-cudnn7-py3 job.
The subset of tests we run are based on the list here, which are the results from running internal queries regarding the test case statuses on Windows vs Linux platforms from the last 30 days. The idea is that if a test case is more likely to fail on Windows than Linux, then it would be counted as a smoke test for Windows.
Originally, our initial query results yielded valid, non-flaky tests, that very much seemed like good smoke tests. Theses results are still the ones used today in CI.
However, our past two query results were not so:
Our second attempt (two weeks ago) ended up with mostly distributed tests, which are known to be flaky.
Our third attempt (last week) ended up with NO test cases satisfying our query. There were no test cases with failures for Windows CUDA only and not also Linux CUDA.
Thus, we should consider what to do as the idea of having smoke tests for Windows seems less practical/realistic now.
Our Options

We could forego our idea of "smoke" tests but still keep the idea of running a subset of tests on PRs. Instead of using a query, we can randomly choose a subset to run. This will save CI cost and potentially maintain signal quality, though research will have to be done to verify that.

1.5 An extension of the first point makes the assumption that there indeed is no idea of smoke tests for Windows. If that's the case, maybe we can further cut costs by sharding our tests and splitting them across our configs randomly. For example, Windows platforms could test 1 shard while Linux would run the other, but who runs what would be randomized. While randomization effectively allows all tests to be covered by all platforms eventually, it introduces nondeterminism and potential frustration in the debugging process of development.

It is possible that there are indeed smoke tests that are more prone to failure on PRs, but maybe they are failed so infrequently that our queries cannot always catch them (as we are confined to the last 30 days). To make this happen, we would need to store and query more long-term stats, or we would have to maintain our own manual list of tests.

🐛 Bug
When define a nn module, and let its member point to a submodule's submodule, then this submodule's weight(s) will appears twice in the model's state_dict. Although there are from the same object (same id).
To Reproduce
Run the following code:
import torch
from torch import nn

class subsubmodule(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, output_size):
        super(subsubmodule, self).__init__()
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(input_size, output_size)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        pass
    
class submodule(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, output_size):
        super(submodule, self).__init__()
        self.emb = subsubmodule(input_size, output_size)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        pass
    
class model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_size, output_size):
        super(model, self).__init__()
        self.encode = submodule(input_size, output_size)
        self.emb = self.encode.emb.emb  # I want to use a shortcut in some case
        
    def forward(self, x):
        pass
    
if __name__ == "__main__":
    a = model(100, 32)
    print(a)
    print("len of state_dict:", len(a.state_dict()))
    for k,v in a.state_dict().items():
        print(k, v.shape)
    print(a.emb is a.encode.emb.emb)

Then it would output
model(
  (encode): submodule(
    (emb): subsubmodule(
      (emb): Embedding(100, 32)
    )
  )
  (emb): Embedding(100, 32)
)
len of state_dict: 2
encode.emb.emb.weight torch.Size([100, 32])
emb.weight torch.Size([100, 32])
True

In a.state_dict(), encode.emb.emb.weight and emb.weight are the same thing but they both appear.
Expected behavior
The same object in model's state_dict() only appears one time (len of a.state_dict() is 1).
As for the print of model, consider about add note such as "ref submodule"? then the print of model would be something like this:
model(
  (encode): submodule(
    (emb): subsubmodule(
      (emb): Embedding(100, 32)
    )
  )
  (emb): Embedding(100, 32) [ref encode.emb.emb]
)

🚀 Feature
Could you please expose torch._aminmax() as an officially supported operation? Thanks!!
Motivation
This operation is needed for hand-rolled runtime quantization. For example, we use it for a large recurrent model to save memory, by quantizing the state tensors to 8 bit. For that, we need to determine the numeric range on a per-tensor basis, which we do currently with _aminmax().
Pitch
torch._aminmax() should become an officially supported API.
Alternatives
The alternatives, besides using the internal API (which works fine!), are to use max(abs()), which creates a full temporary copy in memory, or run max() and min() separately, which requires two data passes.

🚀 Feature
We have an existing optimization pass which optimizes patterns like li = [x, y]; z = li[0] to be z = x. Right now it does not handle list slicing. We saw a case internally in static runtime (cc @hlu1) where the list slice could have been optimized away but was not.
We can extend the logic to handle slice nodes.
@torch.jit.script
def foo(x):
     return [x, 1, 2, 3][0:2]

After running torch._C._jit_pass_peephole(foo.graph) should remove the slice node.
The slice schema is given here. I would suggest looking at Core Program Optimization here.

🐛 Bug
torch.einsum gives incorrect result when implementing an inner product between 1D FloatTensor. I suppose this problem is related to Apple M1 since it gives consistent results on other machines.
To Reproduce
import torch
x = torch.tensor([1., 2.], dtype=torch.float32)
print("float32 : ", torch.einsum('i, i -> ', x, x)) 

y = torch.tensor([1., 2.], dtype=torch.float64)
print("float64 : ", torch.einsum('i, i -> ', y, y)) 

z = torch.tensor([1, 2])
print("int : ", torch.einsum('i, i -> ', z, z))
This gives
float32 :  tensor(0.)
float64 :  tensor(5., dtype=torch.float64)
int :  tensor(5)
